adj:orange.tx: From the noun Orange (“orange fruit”), from French orange.

adj:original.tx: Borrowed from French original, from Old French original, from Late Latin orīginālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, origin”). Doublet of originell.

adv:original.tx: Borrowed from French original, from Old French original, from Late Latin orīginālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, origin”). Doublet of originell.

conj:ohne.tx: From Middle High German āne (“without”), from Old High German āna, ānu, āno (“without”), from Proto-Germanic *ēnu, *ēnō (“without”). Cognate with Yiddish אָן (on), Old Saxon āno (“without”), Old Frisian ōni (“without”), Old Norse án, ón (“without”), English on, ohn (“without”), Gothic 𐌹𐌽𐌿 (inu, “without”), and possibly Ancient Greek ἄνευ (áneu, “without”).

prep:ohne.tx: From Middle High German āne (“without”), from Old High German āna, ānu, āno (“without”), from Proto-Germanic *ēnu, *ēnō (“without”). Cognate with Yiddish אָן (on), Old Saxon āno (“without”), Old Frisian ōni (“without”), Old Norse án, ón (“without”), English on, ohn (“without”), Gothic 𐌹𐌽𐌿 (inu, “without”), and possibly Ancient Greek ἄνευ (áneu, “without”).

adv:ohne.tx: From Middle High German āne (“without”), from Old High German āna, ānu, āno (“without”), from Proto-Germanic *ēnu, *ēnō (“without”). Cognate with Yiddish אָן (on), Old Saxon āno (“without”), Old Frisian ōni (“without”), Old Norse án, ón (“without”), English on, ohn (“without”), Gothic 𐌹𐌽𐌿 (inu, “without”), and possibly Ancient Greek ἄνευ (áneu, “without”).

conj:ob.tx: From Middle High German obe, ob, from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”). Compare English if.

prep:ob.tx: From Middle High German obe, from Old High German oba, from Proto-Germanic *ub (“under”), from Proto-Indo-European *upó (“under, below”). Related with über, oben. A chiefly Upper German word, pronounced with a short vowel in Alemannic areas and with a long vowel in Austro-Bavarian areas. In the north, the short vowel is from etymology 1, perhaps also reinforced by association with regional forms …

adj:out.tx: Borrowed from English out. Doublet of aus.

adj:orthodox.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).

noun:Öl.tx: From Middle High German öl, ol, öle, ole, olei, olge, from Old High German oli, from Proto-West Germanic *oli (“olive oil”). Doublet of Oleum.

noun:Oktave.tx: From Middle High German octāv, from Medieval Latin octava (“eighth”).

adv:oft.tx: From Middle High German ofte, oft, uft, from Old High German ofta, ofto, oftu, from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (“often”). Cognate with Dutch oft, English oft and often.

adj:omnipotent.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.

noun:Ohr.tx: From Middle High German ôre, from Old High German ōra, from Proto-West Germanic *auʀā, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô. Akin to Dutch oor, English ear, West Frisian ear, Swedish öra, all ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ows-. Further Indo-European cognates: Latin auris, Lithuanian ausis, Ancient Greek οὖς (oûs), Russian у́хо (úxo), Old Armenian ունկն (unkn), …

noun:Ordnung.tx: From Middle High German ordenunge, from Old High German ordinunga, from the verb ordinōn (“to put in order”). Equivalent to ordnen + -ung.

adv:ohnehin.tx: Univerbation of ohne (“without”) + hin (“thither, there”), from a sense of "without (even) going there", formed in analogy to mithin in the 18th century.

noun:Opal.tx: From Latin opalus, from Medieval Greek ὀπάλλιος (opállios), from Sanskrit उपल (upala, “gem, stone”).

noun:Oase.tx: 18th century, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Egyptian wḥꜣt. The singular in -e (19th c.) is a backformation from the plural Oasen.

noun:Ohm.tx: From northern Middle High German ōem and Middle Low German ōm, with reduction of the unstressed ultima and regular loss of intervocalic -h- from Old High German ōheim, Old Saxon *ōhēm, from Proto-West Germanic *auhaim (“maternal uncle”).

noun:Oktober.tx: From Middle High German octōber, from Latin Octōber, from octō (“eight”).

noun:Olive.tx: From Latin olīva. Partially inherited through Middle High German olīve (“olive tree”), but both the undiphthongized form and the fact that the use for the fruit dates only from the 16th century show that the word had not been fully integrated in Middle High German times.

noun:Omega.tx: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ὦ μέγα (ô méga) (older called ὦ (ô))

noun:Omnibus.tx: Borrowed from French (voiture) omnibus, from Latin omnibus (“[for] all, everyone”).

noun:Orange.tx: Borrowed from French orange, short for pomme d'orange, from Spanish naranja, from Arabic نَارَنْج (nāranj), from Persian نارنگ (nârang), ultimately from Sanskrit नारङ्ग (nāraṅga, “orange tree”). Doublet of Pomeranze.

noun:Order.tx: Early 17th century, from French ordre. The mercantile sense after English order.

noun:Oregano.tx: 19th century, borrowed from Spanish orégano, at first for the New-World species in the Lippia genus. Use for the Mediterranean plant since the latter half of the 20th century (ca. 1970s).

noun:Origami.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 折り紙 (おりがみ, origami), from 折り (おり, ori, “to fold”) + 紙 (かみ, kami, “paper”).

noun:Os.tx: Borrowed from Latin os, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁.

noun:Otter.tx: From Middle High German otter, from Old High German ottar, from Proto-West Germanic *otr.

intj:oki.tx: Probably a clipping of okidoki, but alternatively analyzable as OK + -i.

noun:Obdach.tx: From Middle High German obedach, from Old High German obdah, obadah (“over-roof, protective roof”); compare oben and Dach.

adj:öffentlich.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German offanlīh (“open, public”) and offanlīhho (“openly, publicly”). Equivalent to offen + -lich.

adj:offen.tx: From Middle High German offen, Old High German offan, ofan, ophan, from Proto-West Germanic *opan. Cognate with Low German open, apen, Dutch open, English open, Danish åben, Swedish öppen. Related to auf.

adv:offen.tx: From Middle High German offen, Old High German offan, ofan, ophan, from Proto-West Germanic *opan. Cognate with Low German open, apen, Dutch open, English open, Danish åben, Swedish öppen. Related to auf.

verb:öffnen.tx: From Middle High German offenen, from Old High German offanōn, from Proto-West Germanic *opanōn, from Proto-Germanic *upanōną. Compare Dutch openen and English open.

noun:Ossi.tx: From a clipping of Osten (“east”) + -i. The form Ossi (instead of *Osti) might suggest a humorous reinterpretation of English Aussie (“Australian person”), although this word has not been widely known in Germany.

noun:Osten.tx: From Ost or Old High German ostan, from Proto-Germanic *austrą, related to *ausos (“dawn”), compare Latin aurora, and Latin auster, which, probably due to a re-orientation, means "South".

noun:Ozean.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin ōceanus, from Ancient Greek ὠκεανός (ōkeanós).

conj:obwohl.tx: Univerbation of ob + wohl, from the older use of ob as a conditional and concessive conjunction, reinforced with an adverb. Compare obgleich, obschon, obzwar and also gleichwohl.

noun:Ohrwurm.tx: From Ohr (“ear”) + Wurm (“worm”). In ancient times, dried and ground animals of the order Dermaptera were used to treat ear diseases, which resulted in the Late Latin name auricula. Later the name was in error explained as “worm that enters the ear”. Consider Dutch oorworm, English earwig, Danish ørentvist; French perce-oreille, Romanian urechelniță; Russian уховёртка (uxovjórtka), Serbo-Croatian …

noun:Obst.tx: From Middle High German obeȥ, from Old High German obaȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *obaet.

noun:Ofen.tx: From Middle High German oven, from Old High German ofan, from Proto-West Germanic *ofn. Cognates See also Dutch oven, Low German Aven, German Low German Aven, Awen, Owen, West Frisian ûne, English oven, Danish ovn, Swedish ugn, Icelandic ofn, Gothic auhns; also Sanskrit उखा (ukhā), Albanian anë, Latin aulla, olla, Ancient Greek ἰπνός (ipnós).

conj:oder.tx: From Middle High German oder (whence also Yiddish אָדער (oder)), from Old High German odar, an alteration of odo by analogy with wedar (whence modern weder). The form odo is an assimilated, unstressed form of eddo (also edo), itself cognate with Old Saxon ettho, Old English eþþa, oþþe, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau). This formation is of uncertain origin: While the second component is Proto-Germanic …

adv:oder.tx: From Middle High German oder (whence also Yiddish אָדער (oder)), from Old High German odar, an alteration of odo by analogy with wedar (whence modern weder). The form odo is an assimilated, unstressed form of eddo (also edo), itself cognate with Old Saxon ettho, Old English eþþa, oþþe, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau). This formation is of uncertain origin: While the second component is Proto-Germanic …

noun:Ost.tx: From Middle High German ōst, from Old High German *ost, from Proto-West Germanic *austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą. Compare Dutch oost, English east, West Frisian east, Norwegian Bokmål øst, Norwegian Nynorsk aust.

noun:Ort.tx: From Middle High German ort (“point (of a tool or weapon), corner, end point, boundary, border, site, place”), from Old High German ort (“point, tip, corner”) (8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *oʀd, from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“point”).

noun:Oberhaupt.tx: From ober- + Haupt. Cognate with Dutch opperhoofd, Danish opperhoved; Norwegian overhode is a calque of the German term (according to ordnett.no).

noun:Ochse.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ohse. Cognate with Dutch os, West Frisian okse, Saterland Frisian Okse, Low German Oss, Plautdietsch Oss, Yiddish אָקס (oks), Icelandic oxi and uxi, Faroese oksi, Norwegian Bokmål okse, Norwegian Nynorsk okse, Swedish oxe, Danish okse, and English ox.

noun:Ohrring.tx: From Middle High German ōrrinc, from Old High German ōrring, from Proto-West Germanic *auʀahring, equivalent to Ohr (“ear”) + Ring (“ring”). Cognate with English earring.

adj:öde.tx: From Middle High German œde, ōde, from Old High German ōdi, from Proto-West Germanic *auþī (“empty, barren”), from Proto-Germanic *auþijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewtyos (“forlorn, deserted”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew (“away from”).

noun:Ostern.tx: From Middle High German ōsteren (plural of ōstere), from Old High German ōstarūn, a plural form of ōstara, from Proto-West Germanic *Austrā, from Proto-Germanic *Austrǭ. Compare English Easter.

noun:Opfer.tx: From Middle High German opfer, from Old High German ophar. Analyzable as a deverbal from opfern.

noun:Öse.tx: First attested in the 15th century in Central German ōse, Middle Low German ôse. Regarding this northern origin, it probably stems from Old Saxon *ōsia, from Proto-West Germanic *ansiju, from Proto-Germanic *ansijō (“loop, handle”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enseh₂- (“loop, hook, handle”). Alternatively, it may be related to Ohr (“ear”); compare Öhr (“eye of the needle”).

adv:oben.tx: From Middle High German oben, obene, from Old High German obana, from Proto-West Germanic *obanā, from Proto-Germanic *ubanē. Related to über and ober-.

noun:Ohropax.tx: From the trademarked product sold in Germany. Originally derived from Ohr and Latin pax (“peace”).

noun:Orang-Utan.tx: Borrowed from English orangutan, from Malay orang utan.

noun:Ökologie.tx: Coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866, öko- + -logie.

noun:Ökonomie.tx: From Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”) (by surface analysis, öko- + -nomie).

noun:Orkan.tx: Borrowed from Dutch orkaan, from Spanish huracán, from Taíno *hurakā. Doublet of Hurrikan.

adj:originell.tx: Borrowed from French originel, from Late Latin originālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin origō (“beginning, source, origin”). Doublet of original.

noun:Öffnung.tx: From Middle High German offenunge, from Old High German offanunga.

noun:Orgasmus.tx: Borrowed from Latin orgasmus, from Ancient Greek ὀργασμός (orgasmós).

noun:Ozon.tx: Coined by Christian Friedrich Schönbein in 1840.

noun:Oheim.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German ōheim, from Proto-West Germanic *auhaim (“maternal uncle”). See dialectal English eam for cognates.

noun:Oberfläche.tx: First attested in the 17th century. From ober- (“upper”) + Fläche (“flat area, surface”), a calque of Latin superficiēs.

noun:Ohrfeige.tx: Ohr (“ear”) + Feige (“fig”), cognate of Dutch oorvijg.

noun:Objekt.tx: From Middle High German object (14th c.), from Latin obiectum.

noun:Obduktion.tx: 18th century, from Latin obductio (“covering, enveloping”). The semantic motivation appears unclear, perhaps from the covering of the body before and after the examination.

noun:Orchidee.tx: Borrowed from French orchidée, from New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis).

noun:Opiat.tx: From Middle High German opiāt, from Latin opiātum.

noun:Orgel.tx: From Middle High German orgel, from Old High German orgela, from Proto-West Germanic *orgalā (“musical instrument”).

noun:Okzident.tx: From Middle High German occident(e), from Latin occidēns, occidentem.

noun:Orthodoxie.tx: From Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía), from ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) + δόξα (dóxa, “way, opinion”).

noun:Odyssee.tx: From Latin Odyssēa, from Ancient Greek Ὀδύσσεια (Odússeia).

noun:Ozelot.tx: Borrowed from French ocelot, from Classical Nahuatl ocelotl.

noun:Onanie.tx: From New Latin onania, after the biblical character Onan. Compare English onanism and Hebrew אוננות (onanút).

noun:Ökonom.tx: From Late Latin oeconomus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonómos)

verb:opfern.tx: From Middle High German opfern, ophern, from Old High German opfarōn, opharōn, offarōn, from Medieval Latin operor (“work”) and/or Medieval Latin offerō (“offer”).

verb:ordnen.tx: From Middle High German ordenen, from Old High German ordinōn, from Proto-West Germanic *ordinōn (“to order, put in order”). Doublet of ordinieren.

noun:Oleander.tx: From French oléandre, or Italian oleandro.

conj:obgleich.tx: Univerbation of ob + gleich, from the older use of ob as a conditional and concessive conjunction, reinforced with an adverb. Compare obwohl, obschon, obzwar and also gleichwohl.

adj:ohrenbetäubend.tx: From Ohr + -en- + betäubend, literally “ear-deafening, ear-numbing”. (The verb is used here in its obsolete sense “to deafen”, but it can also be read with the modern sense “to numb”.) Compare Dutch oorverdovend.

noun:Ott.tx: Shortened from Germanic names containing the element *aud (“riches”). See also Otto.

noun:Orchester.tx: 18th century, from French orchestre, from Latin orchestra, from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra). Based on the pronunciation rules for Greek words the form with /ç/ is expected (see Orchidee), but the more common /k/ follows the French usage.

verb:organisieren.tx: From French organiser + -ieren. Cognate with Hunsrik organiseere.

verb:orientieren.tx: Borrowed from French orienter. Cognate with Hunsrik orïenteere.

noun:Offizier.tx: Borrowed from Middle French officier (from the 16th century), from Medieval Latin officiārius.

noun:Olympiade.tx: Ultimately from the inflected stem of Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπιάς (Olumpiás).

intj:oje.tx: Short for o Jesus. Compare the fuller ojemine, from o Jesu Domine.

verb:ordern.tx: Late 17th century (in the obsolete sense) from Order + -n. The modern sense developed in merchant parlance after English to order.

adv:obendrein.tx: * Univerbation of oben + darein, also analyzable as oben + drein.

noun:Orthographie.tx: Borrowed from Latin orthographia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (orthogrăphĭ́ā).

adj:oberflächlich.tx: Oberfläche + -lich Could be a calque of Latin superficiālis. Attested since the 18th century.

noun:Oberhand.tx: Inherited from Middle High German oberhant. By surface analysis, ober + Hand.

verb:observieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin observāre in the 16th century.

conj:obschon.tx: Univerbation of ob + schon, from the older use of ob as a conditional and concessive conjunction, reinforced with an adverb. Compare obwohl, obgleich, obzwar.

noun:Ortolan.tx: Borrowed from Italian ortolano, from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”).

noun:Oberst.tx: From Middle High German ob(e)rest, ob(e)rōst, ob(e)rist, öbrist, from Old High German obarōsto, obaristo, superlative of Old High German obaro.

noun:Obolus.tx: Borrowed from Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós).

verb:operieren.tx: From Latin operārī (“to work, labor, toil, have effect”) + -ieren, from opus, operis (“work, labor”). Cognate with Hunsrik opereere.

verb:orgeln.tx: From Middle High German orgelen, equivalent to Orgel + -n.

adj:ordentlich.tx: Equivalent to ordnen (“to put in order”) + -lich.

noun:Orvieto.tx: From Italian Orvieto, from Latin Urbs Vetus (literally “old city”).

adj:ominös.tx: Borrowed from French omineux, from Latin ōminōsus. Analysable as Omen + -ös.

adj:oll.tx: From German Low German oll-, the inflected stem of old/olt (“old”), from Middle Low German olt, from Old Saxon ald. Doublet of alt. Cognate with English old, which see for more. For usage, compare English ol'.

noun:Ottonormalverbraucher.tx: Otto + Normalverbraucher, popularised by the film Berliner Ballade (1948).

noun:ODESSA.tx: Acronym of Organisation der ehemaligen SS-Angehörigen.

adv:öfter.tx: From Middle High German ofter, from Old High German oftor.

adj:ohnmächtig.tx: From late Middle High German ōnmehtig, ōmehtig, a variant of earlier ānmehtic, from Old High German āmahtīg. By surface analysis, ohne + -mächtig or Ohnmacht + -ig.

noun:Ohnmacht.tx: From Middle High German ānmaht, an alteration (due to ān, āne ("without"; > German ohne)) of āmaht, from Old High German *āmaht, suggested by āmahtīg (“powerless”), from ā- (“without”) + maht. Compare Old High German unmaht. More at unmight.

noun:Ödem.tx: From New Latin edema, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”).

verb:oxidieren.tx: Borrowed from French oxyder. By surface analysis, Oxid + -ieren.

noun:Ostersonntag.tx: Ostern + Sonntag with a clipping of the -n.

noun:Olympiasieger.tx: From Olympia (“Olympia; the Olympics”) + Sieger (“winner, victor”).

noun:Odem.tx: Central and Low German variant of Atem (“breath”) with the widespread dialectal development -ā- → -ō- and unshifted -d-; compare Middle Low German ādem. The form was spread through Luther’s Bible translation but did not replace the Upper German Atem in the everyday sense.

noun:Objektiv.tx: Since the first half of the 19th century, originally a clipping of Objektivglas (since the 18th century). Compare also French objectif and verre objectif.

noun:Ordnungswidrigkeit.tx: From ordnungswidrig (“contrary to [public] order”) + -keit (“-ness, -ty”). Further analysable as Ordnung (“order”) + -s- + widrig (“contrary”) + -keit.

noun:Ölbaum.tx: From Middle High German öl(e)boum, from Old High German oliboum. By surface analysis, Öl + Baum, literally “oil tree”. Compare archaic Ölbeere (“olive”).

verb:obsen.tx: * Medial clipping (truncation, shortening) of the verb observieren

noun:Ocker.tx: From Middle High German ocker, ogger, from Old High German ockar, from Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”), from ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale, ocher”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).

noun:Oblate.tx: From Middle High German oblāte f, oblāt f, from Old High German oblāta, from Late Latin oblāta (“offered”), past participle of offerō.

noun:Öde.tx: From Old High German ōdi (“empty, deserted”), from Proto-West Germanic *auþī. Cognate to Old English ēaþe, īeþe and Old Norse auðr.

noun:Opus.tx: 17th century, from Latin opus. Doublet of Oper and Œuvre.

adj:originär.tx: From French originaire, from Latin orīginārius.

noun:Ölauge.tx: Öl (“oil”) + Auge (“eye”). The racial slur is probably due to the often slightly yellowish sclera in dark-skinned people.

noun:Ochsenauge.tx: Ochse (“ox”) + Auge (“eye”). Compare Czech volské oko and Finnish häränsilmä.

noun:Odel.tx: From Middle High German atel, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *adalaz. Cognate with English addle (“putrid”).

verb:obliegen.tx: From Middle High German obligen, obeligen, obe ligen, from Old High German oba liggen (“to lie on top of”). By surface analysis, ob- + liegen. Cognate with Middle Low German obeliggen.

noun:Olm.tx: From Middle High German olm, from Old High German olm. Further etymology unknown. Cognate with Middle Dutch olm.

noun:Obmann.tx: From Middle High German obeman, equivalent to ob- (“over-”) + Mann (“man”).

noun:Ochsenzunge.tx: From Old High German ochsenzunga. Equivalent to Ochse + -n- + Zunge.

noun:Otterngezücht.tx: From Otter (“adder”) + Gezücht (“brood”). Ultimately a calque of Ancient Greek γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν (gennḗmata ekhidnôn).

noun:One-Night-Stand.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English one-night stand

noun:Obstgarten.tx: From Middle High German obezgarte, from Old High German obazgarto. Equivalent to Obst + Garten.

intj:ojemine.tx: From Latin o Jesu Domine (“o Lord Jesus!”).

noun:Operateur.tx: From Operation + -eur and from French opérateur.

noun:Oligarch.tx: From Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs), from ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) + άρχης (árkhēs, “ruler”, “leader”).

noun:Ortsgruppenleiter.tx: From Ort (“place, location”) + -s- + Gruppe (“group”) + -n- + Leiter (“head, director, leader”).

noun:Öre.tx: Borrowed from Swedish öre and Danish øre, from Proto-Germanic *aurijaz, from Latin aureus.

noun:Ohrmuschel.tx: From Ohr + Muschel. Compare Dutch oorschelp, Russian ушна́я ра́ковина (ušnája rákovina).

noun:Oberhemd.tx: From ober- (“upper”) + Hemd (“shirt”). Compare Dutch overhemd.

intj:Oida.tx: Borrowed from Bavarian oida. Piecewise doublet of Alter.

adv:obendrauf.tx: * Univerbation of oben + darauf, also analyzable as oben + drauf.

noun:Okra.tx: From an unknown West African language, perhaps via English okra.

intj:öff.tx: Onomatopoeic. Compare Danish øf, Swedish nöff, Hungarian röf.

adj:ordnungswidrig.tx: From Ordnung + -s- + widrig, literally “contrary to [public] order”.

phrase:Operation gelungen, Patient tot.tx: Literally, “operation successful, patient dead”. After a 19th-century medical joke. Compare Danish operationen lykkedes, men patienten døde.

noun:Ölung.tx: Middle High German ölunge, by surface analysis, ölen + -ung.

noun:Obsession.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin obsessiōnis, influenced by English obsession.
